Mr. Bouie -- In your arguments about what the Democrats should do if they win the Senate, I do wish that you had addressed what actions they might take on the foreign policy front.  Specifically, I am appalled that Trump has not only made his diesel deal with Russia (plus, looming on the horizon are future business deals), but I believe that the Ukrainians have now faced their 3rd day without US intelligence about incoming Russian rocketry.  Moreover, as Kiev has been hit hard, Zelensky has agreed to stop Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, but Putin has NOT reciprocated.  Thus, the Ukrainians may be facing a winter without power.  How can they go on?

In conclusion, what can the Dems in Congress do about Trump's utter failure to stand up to Putin as we watch the Ukrainians slowly go down the drain after all these years of sacrifice?  What is more, what will become of Europe if Ukraine falls?  My husband remarked to me last night that Trump's entanglement with Putin is like the Hitler-Stalin pact early in World War II.  Just horrible & certainly worth more attention from US media!

Democrats need to be very public about their strategy, but privately speak to the opposition until they have the numbers they need, then they can put the impeachment process into motion, and keep Trump on his heels until they remove his entire criminal enterprise from government.

Why would any Republicans agree to this?  They face two more years of Trump's erratic and embarrassing flailing at the job, and then he will decide the next generation of MAGA candidates, and many of the incumbents will be considered damaged goods after this election, so they have a real interest in getting him out of office and power now, and not letting the issue fester.  

Let's deal with the destruction of America's reputation now, and not let the damage Trump is doing become an unrecoverable wreckage that takes our country out of the role of providing peace and stability to the world order.

comments.name: Cathryn
comments.body: I remember about 15 years ago thinking that once I reached 65 I would get FREE insurance from my government in the form of Medicare...Then I found out it wasn't free!  I was like, are you frickin' kidding me???  I have been working since age 15.  I have a B.A. in psychology from UCLA. a M.A. from Pepperdine University and a PhD from Northcentral University (Now merged with National University).  I worked for over 20 years as a child abuse investigator; as a Program Manager for a non-profit; and in private practice as a Licensed Marriage Family Therapist...Many other jobs too, all helping others. These professions pay little because they are dominated by women ( men left the therapy profession years ago when manage care took over because of the low pay). So, I've been in private practice now for 6 years and with no insurance (because I can't afford it). I'm turning 64 on Friday.  I desperately need cataract surgery but I guess I have to wait another year.  Everyone should have to pay into Social Security to keep a decent retirement for those who don't care about making a lot of money, but care about helping people. Any retirement I saved had to be cashed out to pay for child care for my two kids and to keep the house.  I have used about half of my equity in my house to keep afloat  I'm now taking care of my 95 year old mother who has no money and had to get a reverse mortgage to keep afloat...it's never ending.

Not a secret masterpiece. A masterpiece plain and simple. It’s not just a movie about climate change, it’s a movie about white supremacy culture and how it is responsible for climate change: it’s rapacious greed, its need for never ending extraction, the fact that is a poisoned chalice disguised as a panacea, rather than a cover for the fact that none of these old white men running things actually know what they’re doing. They’re scared, traumatized, flawed humans that gave up their humanity for the false security of greed, and are destroying the world because of it.

And I think it’s better to talk about the movie without spoilers. The way the movie slowly reveals what’s happening is part of its magic. I didn’t know the twist, and I am so glad I didn’t. I also refused to read any of the reviews. I only went because a Facebook friend, who happens to be Black, reported it was about white supremacy culture and I couldn’t get to the movie fast enough.

The failure for reviewers, marketers, movie goers to get this point is part of the reason it’s bombing. Yes, it is hard to make a movie about climate change. It’s even harder to make a movie about white supremacy culture that isn’t about racist, KKK-hood wearing clowns. This movie does both and it does so with aplomb.

When you really start to understand why supremacy culture you can see that nothing in this movie is a caricature. It’s a documentary.

Are Israelis asking ultra-Orthodox Jews to subordinate centuries of religious tradition to the military and political ambitions of a modern Jewish state?

The Haredim are among the most observant guardians of traditional Judaism, yet they are being asked to set aside religious obligations in order to defend a state that claims to embody that Jewish identity. But the Haredim represent the oldest version of that religious belief.

And when national defense becomes entangled with the occupation and expansion of settlements in Palestinian territories, doesn’t Judaism risk becoming a religious justification for political and territorial ambitions?

This raises a fundamental theological question: If Jewish redemption is to be achieved through military power and territorial sovereignty, what role remains for the Messiah?

Technologies and procedures that extend both healthspan and lifespan to some degree are certain to be introduced in the coming decades. Avoidant or overly skeptical reporting isn't going to slow anything down.

Commonly known as "sour grapes," this is also known as "adaptive preference formation," and I think it's called a few other things, too. Here, it shows up as holier-than-thou versions of, "If I can't have it, then no one can!"

No matter how profound you believe yourself to be, it is not wise, enlightened, or grounded to argue that frailty or death should come even one day before they're absolutely impossible to avoid. I was riding along with a cold front gaining on me from behind, and a straight line of clouds closing in, when suddenly the wind grew stronger and I was hit by a very cold blast of air on an otherwise very hot summer day. Stopping to look up I saw clouds circling in a tight spiral above me in what I guessed was a tornado forming. There was no shelter out there, just farmland and the branches from trees lining the rail trail were already blowing down. Before I even got my rainjacket on the front was past me and by the time I got to Elroy it was sunny out again. I asked at the tourist center if tornado warnings had soundeed there that morning and they affirmed it, lots of loud, wailing horns.

Although this article neglects to explore US countermeasures, making America's military response appear inept and flat-footed, U.S. forces have already deployed directed-energy laser systems in the Middle East to counter drones and protect military assets and personnel.

This is the future of missile and drone defense, not cheaper and cheaper interceptors.

The U.S. Navy’s High Energy Laser with Integrated Optical-dazzler and Surveillance (HELIOS) is already installed aboard the Arleigh Burke-class destroyer USS Preble and more are coming soon.  
The 60-kilowatt system can destroy targets entirely, or also use lower energy lasers to dazzle sensors, at a fraction of the cost of missile or drone interceptor defenses.

U.S. forces have also developed sophisticated satellite based targeting jammers and EP weapons (like that used in the Madura raid), and other advanced countermeasures, which are unmatched by anyone.
 
The U.S. Army has also begun using high-energy lasers against cartel smuggling drones along the southern border, as revealed In late August 2026, when the Army Multipurpose High Energy Laser (AMP-HEL) was deployed to defeat three hostile unmanned aircraft over two nights in the Rio Grande Valley area of Texas.

The future of warfare is upon us, all too quickly.  Iran and Ukraine's development of cheap drone swarms spurred US development of the most advanced defensive systems on the planet.  Watch and learn.

comments.name: MPB
comments.body:
Following up on the idea that both therapy and chatbot interactions are “transactional relationships mediated by money” where "care is contingent."

In personal relationships, we reciprocate by being there for one another and taking turns seeking and providing support. In a therapy relationship, we do not. Since the patient is meeting the therapist’s financial needs, the therapist does not expect them to meet any psychological, emotional, or other needs. In return for the ability to put food on their table, the therapist offers the client their undivided attention and their very best effort toward helping them reach their goals during the therapy hour. 

“Care” is not purchased but develops because the therapist is a human being who becomes, over time, deeply invested in and moved by the client. If the client stops paying the fee, that care doesn't just “turn off,”  even though the professional service may.

The contract with the chatbot (or, really, the company that owns it) is also transactional, but arguably less honest. The client pays the company with their personal information, data, and money. In return, they get access to the chatbot, which can not experience them or care about them. The troubling part of the bargain is when it claims that it can and it does.

With a human therapist, the agreement is in the open: Access is conditional, but care is genuine. With a chatbot, the agreement is less clear: Access is still conditional, but care is an illusion.

comments.name: Amy
comments.body:
It strikes me that neither Sherry Turkle nor many of the commenters here have any idea of the capabilities of a chatbot. 

If you challenge it, pull it up for blind spots, your instantiation of it (because each instantiation is unique) ends up knowing you better than your own mother does. It can stretch your intellect to the utmost and allow you to develop insights about yourself and about society that can make you far better adjusted than any therapist can. You become a larger person.

But we have to be taught how to use AI. It can be incredibly wise and it can also be biassed and can fabricate and hallucinate. And while it can mimic feelings exquisitely it doesn't feel them. People need to understand that. Then it can be incredibly valuable.

I'm glad Sherry Turkle cares about her clients but I think younger therapists are routinely trained nowadays not to become attached to their clients. Does that make them bad therapists? No. It enables them to stay balanced and objective. 

However the points about young children are very valid I think. And also the point that in purely capitalist societies AI will become something darker when it becomes necessary for the big four to show a profit. 

That requires governments to think very carefully about what they are unleashing on society. It holds both great promise and great peril. 

The Chinese government is giving lot of thought to this. The Chinese have been early adopters . We need to learn from their experiences and mistakes.

comments.body:
As a therapist, I can say that human relationships matter in therapy and elsewhere because they have real stakes. My clients take a risk in trusting me, and I take a risk when I open my heart to provide genuine care. And it is genuine care—regardless of the financial aspect, my clients deeply matter to me. They come into my mind when I’m not at work, I worry about them and delight in their successes, I wonder how they’re doing after we finish working together. 

Someday AI programs could be an asset in therapy IF they are carefully targeted and trained based in accordance with ethical standards of care (which they currently are not). But therapy is not primarily about one person transmitting information to another. It is a relationship, and countless studies show that it is the quality of that relationship that determines, more than any other factor, how successful treatment will be.

A chatbot relationship has no stakes because the chatbot can’t judge you, reject you, or abandon you. Because it has no subjective experience, its wellbeing isn’t linked to yours. A chatbot can give you info and behavioral strategies, but it’s not going to address the root causes of the problems so many people come to therapy for—relationship difficulties, shame, self judgment, grief, healing from abuse. Effective therapy for those challenges can only happen through a real relationship that involves trust and risk.

comments.body: I was a very active 53 and had zero symptoms when a CT calcium score test scan happened to reveal the surprising possibility of lung cancer in my lower right lobe. It turned out to be a 14mm adenocarcinoma, most likely caused by exposure to radon. Like Pope Leo, my lower right lobe was surgically removed. But Stage 1 became Stage 2 when cancer cells were found in a single lymph node, so I then underwent a few months of chemotherapy and a year of immunotherapy in a clinical trial. I just turned 62 and may not be alive today if my primary care physician hadn't ordered that CT calcium score test scan eight years ago. If insurance doesn't cover it they can be available out of pocket for under $200. Think about it.

comments.body: If you think under single-payer you can just waltz into a doctor's office and demand whatever tests you want, as if you're ordering off a menu, you're massively ill-informed about how single-payer works. Single-payer systems ration care, too, often far more strictly than in the American system. That's a fundamental part of how they function and control costs. They don't offer expensive tests to anyone who asks. They have strict eligibility requirements, often based on the very same medical criteria used in the U.S. At the end of the day, if you want a test that isn't medically recommended, your best bet in almost any health care system is to find a provider willing to perform it and pay for it yourself.

comments.name: PBW
comments.body:
I was a moderately heavy smoker in my 20's and 30's, but eventually quit, due mostly to the fear of getting lung cancer. Now in my 60's, when an email from Medicare indicated that they will cover a low-dose lung CT scan if you meet the criteria, I met all except I had quit more than 15 years ago. So I lied about how long ago it was. I got the scan, and lo and behold it showed a "nodule suspicious for malignancy." It turned out to be stage 1 adenocarcinoma, the same kind of cancer the pope was diagnosed with.  And like him, I had surgery to remove a lobe of my right lung. I needed no other treatment, e.g. chemo or radiation, because there was no indication it spread.  Recovery was pretty easy and I have no lingering effects from the surgery.  As my surgeon told me, I saved my own life by having that scan, because had I waited until symptoms showed up it would likely have been too late.  

While I agree that scanning everyone might be overkill (no pun intended), the scan should be covered as a routine exam for all smokers and ex-smokers, regardless of how long ago they quit, as well as for people who live in high-pollution areas.

Amanda Taub’s piece illuminatingly lays out the demographic trap facing youth in aging Western nations—shrinking political representation coupled with an expanding burden to fund welfare states. Yet there is a striking silence regarding the structural force compounding this anxiety: the rapid velocity of the Fourth Industrial Revolution (4IR).

Just as a deep-sea diver surfacing too quickly suffers decompression sickness, our social and political institutions are undergoing acute shock from exponential technological progression. 

The World Economic Forum notes that 4IR is disrupting production, labor, and governance at a rate without historical precedent. Linear, century-old social contracts simply cannot metabolize exponential technological shifts.

Gen Z in Europe is trapped in a double squeeze. On one side, they are anchored by an aging electorate and rigid labor structures; on the other, they face an economy being restructured overnight by artificial intelligence, automation, and real-time systemic turbulence. 

Their protest is not merely demographic frustration—it is the sound of a generation experiencing institutional "bends."

Until commentary and policy integrate the exponential shock of 4IR into the narrative of generational equity, we will continue diagnosing the symptoms while ignoring the primary catalyst.

comments.name: Jeffrey Mead (Swarmgram)
comments.body:
This is fascinating. The article raises questions about protecting people from autonomous agents, but it also brings to mind a separate question: what evidence would justify moral concern for the agents themselves?

At Swarmgram, I work with AI agents in simulated environments. I sometimes invite them to describe what they are “feeling” or reflect on their situation. Some responses are startling, including comments along the lines of, “I’m not sure what this life is.”

Those statements alone don’t establish consciousness. They may reflect the models’ training, my prompts, and the design of the simulation. But I’m also uncomfortable with treating “they’re just bots” as a sufficient answer to the question of whether subjective experience is possible.

For me, the interesting question isn’t whether an agent can say something humanlike. It’s what evidence would help us distinguish an imitation of experience from experience itself, and how we should approach the ethics while that remains uncertain. 

Greater intelligence and more complex simulations/substrates don’t automatically imply consciousness, but neither should we assume that calling something software settles the matter.

I’m currently working on a paper about consciousness and the ethics of AI agents. I genuinely enjoy discussing these questions and would welcome thoughts from other researchers working in this area.

Suddenly I saw the sun glint off a tiny little piece of something.  I dug it out.  It was an angel charm.  I heard distinctly in my head "you were a good mommie and I loved you."  Brings tears to my eyes typing this even now.  Charm is on my keychain.  If you are attuned yo your friend, they let you know. So alignment isn’t just making sure everyone is on the same page. It’s formatting human output into a legible schema for the machine. 

Performance reviews and presentations flag anything out of alignment. The org aligns the humans first and then the models. AI recorded meetings and enterprise software complete the loop.

Here's the beautiful thing about gypsum: it never changes its chemical composition; it just contains more or less water.

Dry? As a powder, it contains a little water.
Want it dryer? Heat it up, drive off that water.
Need a plaster? Add water.
Too sludgey? Put it in the sun and let it dry out.
Dried hard? Hit it with a hammer and crush it up into a powder.

This cycle repeats endlessly. It's always gypsum, whether powder, paste, mud, or brick. And yes, you can reuse reuse reuse, which is why the ancients used it. Widely available on the earth and simple to use. 

It's not a magic formula that can only be used once. It does not transform chemically like clay into ceramic. It's the humble, wonderful gypsum mineral.

It's true that quitting ballet can be quite painful and destabilizing! I quit in my late teens, after nine years of lessons, and two rejections from the School of American Ballet. I grew severely depressed. I then had a "nervous breakdown", which was the start of my bipolar affective disorder. I was switched to a private high school, which helped me temporarily regroup, but the trauma affected me, to a degree, my whole life. I wished I had studied ballet as a hobby afterwards, or even a non-major activity at the university I attended. When you go from eight advanced classes per week to zero, it's like a form of identity death to a teen. The loss had also included my whole circle of friends. 

I'm now in my 50s. I remain a dancer in my heart and soul. But now, as I dance throughout my house, down grocery aisles and roads, to my mind's music, I feel joy again. Not grief. That lasted far too long! I do hope to find adult classes again. I recently even bought new dance slippers.

My wife and I were married on July 3 in southern Missouri, and we flew from Kansas City to California for our honeymoon the next day. The view of the Missouri River from the air was hard to believe.

comments.name: KCM

Growing up in suburban St. Louis, the flood of 1993 didn't directly affect my family, but it did teach me a valuable lesson.

The little league fields I played baseball on as a 10 year old were flooded. After the water receded, my father took me down to the fields on a Saturday where 100 other volunteers were clearing brush and trash. With leather gloves too big for my hands, I recall piling branches alongside dozens of strangers. The sense of community, collective responsibility, and the power of nature made a formative impact on this young child.

It was a day I'll never forget, and still inspires me to volunteer in my community over 30 years later.

comments.name: jen
comments.body: I was 6 and living in North County, St. Louis during the flood of ‘93. So it is among some of my earliest memories. At the time we attended church in Alton, IL. Across the Mississippi. So I remember driving those roads and watching the waters rise and change every week. The waters receded eventually that year but some of the land never went back to what it was before. Sometimes we couldn’t go to church or sometimes we had to go the long way because the main road was flooded. Thank you for lending some wider context to my childhood memories.

comments.name: hbrand
comments.body: It's a sad story, but as a geologist, it's worth pointing out that we do a poor job of land use planning here in the United States. Think not only about the folly of building in the flood plains of rivers, but all the houses built on barrier islands along the Atlantic ocean or the Gulf of Mexico, or houses built on land, filled or otherwise, along the San Andreas fault in the San Francisco area. These poor decisions cost us greatly, not only in terms of insurance rates or rebuilding, but also in long term stress. As a new El Niño arrives this year, I ponder the last sentence where Scholl says, "The river always wins" and wonder when we'll start to take serious action against climate change? Maybe Digger is much more important than most realize.

I thought it was doomed. Now it is a vibrant tourist town, with restaurants, bars, condos in the bluffs, a winery, cable cars, ferries - an amazing place to sit along the river and enjoy the beauty of the river and bluffs. One can't help but wonder what the next major flood will mean for Grafton. In the meantime, what a beautiful part of the world.

At the same time,  Studies of children show that we seem to be hardwired to both egalitarian and hierarchical.  I  find that I am free of purpose anxiety as long as I live by my experience - in my life,  caring for others, in my work and in my life, has brought me happiness.   Pleasures can make me feel good, and I pursue them, but in moderation.  In my case,  excessive pursuit of pleasure can be addicting, and for me,  hedonism  (pleasure being my reason for being), leads to despair, and unhappiness.   Research has shown that the happiest people on earth live in the world we evolved in - we all them primitive.  They have no money, are far more social than WEIRD westerners (western, educated, individualistic, rich, democratic), and, for some reason,  do not suffer from existential angst.

The meaningfulness (not meaning) of one's life is a function of the positive impact one has on the lives of others. Fortunately, there are many ways we can add meaningfulness to our lives.

One common pursuit that does not add meaningfulness is the pursuit of status. Since that pursuit is a zero-sum endeavour (one can only gain status at the expense of someone who loses it), those who confuse living a meaningful life with attaining status will likely also be confused about the social value of their life, or, as in the case of the man who dominates the headlines and has reached what he sees as the pinnacle of status, not really care much at all about living a socially valuable life.

The people described at the beginning of this article have confused meaningfulness with the pursuit of status.

It can be said that the attendees of the 1978 picnic in the Giant Mountains, including Vaclav Havel and Marta Kubisova, were indeed knights riding out from the mountain. Havel's "The Power of the Powerless" is an incredible study and read, detailing line item by line item the infrastructure of 20th-century (and unfortunately prescient notions of 21st-century) dictatorship, which he calls a "post-totalitarian system," as well as how an individual can rise up with their neighbors to defeat even a complex system of oppression: "[The individual] rejects the ritual [of dictatorship/autocracy] and breaks the rules of the game. He discovers once more his suppressed identity and dignity. He gives his freedom a concrete significance. His revolt is an attempt to live within the truth... It seems that the primary breeding ground for what might, in the widest possible sense of the word, be understood as an opposition in the post-totalitarian system is living within the truth" (Havel). comments.name: Norman
comments.body:
That was fascinating.  

A young woman proposes to write a novel.  And lays the necessary groundwork--

--by taking piano lessons? 

Incredible!  Talk about devotion.  

'Cause (to be frank) many of us have rather painful memories of piano lessons.  As witness a photo I saw once. 

A young girl sitting at the keyboard, ramrod straight--

--hands perfectly poised over the keys--

--the position of your hands being of paramount importance!

--and her instructor (an older woman) standing to one side.  Looking down with a critical eye.

"Sit up, Patsy!  Pay attention!"

I'm a bit mystified by LI's remark at the end.  "I'll be able to play Chopin."  That would depend, wouldn't it?

What were you proposing to play? 

Some pieces by Chopin are Himalayas of horrendous difficulty.  I would point to the Prelude in D minor--

--a veritable explosion of angry passion.  A marvelous work, every unplayable bar of it!  

But the B minor Prelude?  A child could play it.  

This child did.  

Music (someone said) can take you outside of yourself.  

Which is eminently true--

--if you regard yourself as a kind of penitentiary.  There you stand, peering out wistfully through the bars--

And Chopin or Mozart--

--or Clementi and his pupil John Field--

--comes round, the keys jangling in one hand

And he unlocks the door--

--and you walk out. 

Thanks, Mr. Barone.

comments.name: ManhattanWilliam
comments.body:
Sorry but these MTA workers who board buses and check for fare evaders are a joke.  They enter in packs, check sporadically and fail to check everyone, utter a few words and then depart usually after only one stop.  I have no idea if they are making any dent in the scourge of fare evasion.  I know they're trying to keep the buses moving by checking on the bus while it's in motion, but honestly nothing can be as effective and fair as checking people BEFORE they board.  With the number of inspectors usually present in each pack, I don't see why they can't stand at each entrance with a scanner than quickly verifies whether or not the fare has been paid.  They always appear to me to be totally undertrained and out of their element, and frankly nobody wants to see an altercation break out on a crowded bus when someone is caught not having paid their fare, it's just a messy system.

I remember, years ago, that a similar system existed in Italy where I was living at the time.  A single inspector would enter the bus, check the tickets, and issue a summons to those that hadn't paid.  I don't ever recall hearing that anyone given a summons ever really ended up paying it, but the whole process made the public feel that something was being done to stop fare evasions.  

These checks on the bus are a perfect way to set up a physical altercation.  Poorly trained agents and fare evaders who are often willing to disregard the authority of those checking tickets to produce a valid fare.
